column1: # SHARED L7 PATH-MATCHING VECTOR TABLE -- ONE file, read by THREE suites.
# The terminate tier (HTTPS, which is ALL git API traffic) is enforced by the
# Python addon; the passthrough/cleartext tier by the Zig proxy. A disagreement
# between the two matchers is a security bug, not a cosmetic one, so both read
# and cogworx (the rule PRODUCER) keeps a byte-identical mirror at
# so no wildcard pattern can be compiled whose semantics are not pinned here.
# Changing one matcher fails its own suite; "fixing" the table for one matcher
# fails the other, because there is only one table.
# TAB-separated. Blank lines and lines starting with `#` are comments.
#       The request-side pipeline: strip at the first `?` or `#`, percent-decode
#       ONCE, then collapse empty segments (trailing slash kept).
#       The normalizer REFUSES the path outright and the caller DENIES the
#       request (403, no credential injected). See the dot-segment block below.
#       The reader normalizes the RAW request path with its own normalizer and
#       then runs its prefix matcher against the rule path verbatim. Rule paths
#       are NEVER normalized -- that asymmetry is deliberate and pinned below.
#       A raw path the normalizer rejects belongs in a `reject` row, not here.
# WILDCARD SEMANTICS. A rule-path segment that is exactly `*` matches EXACTLY
# ONE request segment and never spans a `/`. A segment that is exactly `#` is the
# same thing narrowed to ASCII DIGITS (`[0-9]+`). Either character outside a
# whole segment is a literal, and either one in a REQUEST path is always literal.
# Matching stays boundary-aware left-anchored PREFIX: a rule that ends in a
# wildcard still matches deeper paths, which is why an ALLOW must always
# terminate at a literal segment (see the `/api/v4/projects/*` row).
# TERMINATING AT A LITERAL IS NECESSARY BUT NOT SUFFICIENT -- that is why `#`
# exists. `%2F` decodes into a real separator, so a client-chosen `:id` can
# inflate into several segments, and `*` absorbs the FIRST of them; if the id's
# own LAST component equals the rule's literal tail, the tail is consumed by the
# id and everything after it rides through as ordinary prefix continuation. The
# `tail absorption` block below pins that against the real GitLab shapes. `#`
# closes it for an id that is numeric by construction, because the absorbed
# component would then have to be all digits.
# ---- normalization: query/fragment, empty segments, single-pass decode ----
# Dots INSIDE a segment are ordinary data; only a whole `.`/`..` segment is one.
# %2F DECODES INTO A REAL SEPARATOR. GitLab accepts a URL-encoded project path
# as `:id`, so an encoded slash INFLATES one addressed segment into several --
# the single fact the whole carve-out design turns on.
# Decoding is SINGLE-PASS: %25 -> `%`, never re-decoded into a separator.
# A request may carry a literal `*` or `#`, encoded or not. It stays data. A raw
# `#` is a FRAGMENT delimiter and is stripped with everything after it, so the
# only way one reaches a segment is percent-encoded.
# ---- dot segments are REFUSED, never collapsed ----
# The enforcer decides on the NORMALIZED path but forwards the RAW one upstream,
# so no normalization step may let those two strings name different resources.
# Decoding is safe in that respect: `%2F` becomes a real separator, so it can
# only ever ADD segments, which NARROWS a left-anchored rule. Popping `..` is the
# one step that SUBTRACTS -- and `..%2F` puts it under the client's control, so a
# raw path lexically under a DENY normalizes INTO an ALLOW while the origin stays
# free to route the raw form. Refusing keeps "normalization only adds segments"
# true; nothing in the GitLab REST API or git smart-HTTP needs a dot segment.

column1: # ---- TAIL ABSORPTION: why those allows use `#` and not `*` ----
# GitLab's `:id` is "ID or URL-encoded path", so the sandbox CHOOSES it. Pick an
# encoded path whose LAST component is the rule's own literal tail and `*` eats
# the first component, the tail is satisfied by the id's second, and the real
# resource rides through as prefix continuation -- reaching a token mint on a
# project named `issues` in any namespace the caller controls (push-to-create
# makes one). The paired tail deny misses the same request. `#` fails closed on
# all of it because a namespace component is not digits.

column5: `*` ABSORBS the tail: the allow reaches a token mint
...and the paired deny misses the very same request

column1: # Residual, pinned so it is not forgotten: `#` narrows the absorbed component to
# digits, it does not abolish absorption. A project at `<all-digit-namespace>/issues`
# is still reachable, and this residual is LIVE, not theoretical -- MEASURED against
# a real GitLab 18.5.7 on 2026-08-02, every step, not reasoned about:
# An earlier version of this comment claimed such a namespace would be
# "unaddressable by path, therefore theoretical". That is wrong, and wrong in an
# instructive way: it is TRUE that a bare numeric `:id` resolves as an ID (GET
# /api/v4/groups/99 looks up group id 99, not the group whose path is "99"), which
# is what makes the claim sound right. But the attack does not use a bare segment --
# it uses a TWO-segment path, and GitLab resolves `:id` as a PATH whenever it
# contains a `/`. So `99%2Fissues` addresses the project fine.
# What actually bounds the severity: nothing prevents such a namespace, and any user
# with group-creation rights can make one cheaply, but none exists on the deployment
# instance today (0 all-numeric among 255 top-level namespaces) and the SANDBOX
# cannot create one under this tier -- it would need an attacker with group-creation
# rights on the host plus a compromised agent already holding an issues/mr grant.
# The absolute fix is for the matcher to see the RAW segment and refuse an encoded
# slash inside a wildcard; deliberately not done here.

column5: the named residual: an ALL-DIGIT namespace component
